description: I am D. Jamal Asraf, Founder of Space Hover & CGT, pursuing Aeronautical Engineering. I build aerospace simulations and full-stack web applications. Join our team to build an intuitive Lunar Landing Site Navigator for NASA Space Apps. We combine first-principles engineering with rapid prototyping. Seeking members skilled in orbital mechanics, GIS/LOLA topography, 3D visualization, and web development. Inshallah, let's build a mission-critical tool
summary:
LLSN SKY_X is our NASA Space Apps Challenge project, a web tool for looking at lunar landing sites. You spin a 3D Moon, pick a past landing site or a CLPS target (or type in your own coordinates), set a UTC date and time, and the app shows where the Sun and Earth sit in the sky from that exact spot. There’s also a 30-day timeline you can scrub through and an elevation reading for the site.

We built it because the south pole is hard to plan around. The Sun hangs close to the horizon, shadows get long, and some craters never see sunlight at all. A small change in position or date can change the lighting completely. Earth might look visible on paper but be blocked by a crater wall or ridge, so geometry alone doesn’t tell you much.

The data is real. Sun and Earth positions come from JPL Horizons, the globe texture and terrain from NASA Moon Trek (LRO imagery), and elevation from LOLA. The list of past missions is static, copied from our LLSN brief. The lander descent animation is only for illustration.

It’s still a prototype. Live requests run through a local Vite proxy, so a deployed version would need a server-side proxy. Next we want a terrain-based horizon, proper line-of-sight checks, a resource layer, and confidence labels. We don’t claim it’s safe for real mission decisions.

No one can guarantee a text will never be flagged by an AI detector, since those tools are unreliable. The safest way to make it yours is to change a few phrases into how your team actually talks.
